group.title: Collocations
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To decide what is true after thinking about the facts.
examples: It’s too early to {draw a conclusion} from these results.
wrong: She drew a conclusion before looking at any of the facts, and it was well supported.

words.meaning: To finally agree after discussing something.
examples: After hours of talks, they {reached an agreement}.
wrong: They reached an agreement and still disagreed on every point.

words.meaning: To think about something when making a decision.
examples: We must {take into account} the cost of transport.
wrong: I took the weather into account and forgot about it completely.

words.meaning: To help people know more about a problem.
examples: The campaign aims to {raise awareness} of water waste.
wrong: The poster raised awareness by hiding the facts from everyone.

words.meaning: To finish something by the time it must be done.
examples: We worked late to {meet the deadline}.
wrong: He met the deadline by handing it in a week late.

words.meaning: To remember and think about something.
examples: {Bear in mind} that the shop closes at six.
wrong: Bear in mind the closing time, then forget it.

words.meaning: To get someone’s attention.
examples: A red dress in the window {caught my eye}.
wrong: The bright sign caught my eye, so I didn’t notice it.

words.meaning: To slowly accept a sad or difficult situation.
examples: It took him years to {come to terms with} the loss.
wrong: She came to terms with the change by refusing to accept it.

words.meaning: To cause more problems than it helps.
examples: Too much exercise can {do more harm than good}.
wrong: The medicine did more harm than good, so I felt much better.

words.meaning: To learn skills by doing something.
examples: Volunteering helped her {gain experience} with children.
wrong: He gained experience by never trying the job.

words.meaning: To stop knowing where something is or what is happening.
examples: I {lost track of} time while reading.
wrong: I lost track of the score, so I knew it exactly.

words.meaning: To show too much worry, anger or excitement about something small.
examples: Please don’t {make a fuss}; it’s only a small scratch.
wrong: She made a fuss by calmly saying nothing at all.

words.meaning: To be a possible danger to someone or something.
examples: Rising water levels {pose a threat} to the village.
wrong: The tiny kitten posed a threat to the whole army.

words.meaning: To be in a situation where something bad could happen.
examples: If you don’t back up your files, you {run the risk} of losing them.
wrong: He ran a risk by doing the safest possible thing.

words.meaning: To find a fair middle point between two needs.
examples: It’s hard to {strike a balance} between work and family.
wrong: She struck a balance by giving all her time to work.

words.meaning: To expect something to always be there and not value it.
examples: We often {take clean water for granted}.
wrong: He took his friends for granted and thanked them every day.

words.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, or to wait anxiously.
examples: He {held his breath} as he swam under the water.
wrong: She held her breath by breathing quickly and deeply.

words.meaning: To stop doing something you have done regularly for a long time.
examples: It took me months to {break the habit} of biting my nails.
wrong: She broke the habit of smoking and smoked more than ever.

words.meaning: To make people notice something.
examples: The report {draws attention to} the lack of parks.
wrong: She drew attention to the mistake by keeping it secret.

words.meaning: Very unhappy because something was not as good as hoped.
examples: The fans were {bitterly disappointed} by the loss.
wrong: I was bitterly disappointed with the wonderful gift I wanted.

words.meaning: Very worried about something serious.
examples: Parents are {deeply concerned} about the new road.
wrong: She was deeply concerned, so she didn’t care at all.

words.meaning: Praised by many people as very good.
examples: The new museum is {highly recommended}.
wrong: The hotel is highly recommended, so everyone tells you to avoid it.

words.meaning: Knowing about something completely.
examples: I’m {fully aware} of the risks.
wrong: He was fully aware of the plan, but had never heard of it.

words.meaning: Known by many people.
examples: It’s {widely known} that the old bridge is unsafe.
wrong: The fact is widely known, but only two people know it.

words.meaning: To be one of the causes of something or help it happen.
examples: Luck {played a part} in our success.
wrong: Luck played a part, but had nothing to do with it.

words.meaning: To do something good to make up for a wrong you did.
examples: He tried to {make amends} by buying her flowers.
wrong: She made amends by insulting him again.

words.meaning: To start dealing with a problem.
examples: The council promised to {address the issue} of litter.
wrong: They addressed the issue by ignoring it for years.

words.meaning: To have to deal with something difficult.
examples: Every new team will {face a challenge} in its first year.
wrong: We faced a challenge, an easy task with no problems.

words.meaning: To start to doubt a decision you made.
examples: I’m {having second thoughts} about moving abroad.
wrong: She had second thoughts and felt totally sure of her choice.

words.meaning: To agree by both sides giving up something.
examples: After a long debate, we {reached a compromise}.
wrong: They reached a compromise, and one side got everything it wanted.

words.meaning: To say that you are worried about something.
examples: Doctors have {expressed concern} about the new diet.
wrong: He expressed concern by saying nothing worried him.

words.meaning: To avoid attracting attention.
examples: After the scandal, he {kept a low profile}.
wrong: She kept a low profile by giving interviews on every TV show.

words.meaning: To behave well so others copy you.
examples: Parents should {set a good example} for their children.
wrong: He set an example by doing everything his rules banned.

words.meaning: To see how two things are not the same.
examples: Can you {tell the difference} between the twins?
wrong: I can tell the difference, so they look identical to me.

words.meaning: To say something nice about someone.
examples: It costs nothing to {pay a compliment} to a colleague.
wrong: She paid me a compliment by calling my work rubbish.

words.meaning: To suddenly become very angry.
examples: The coach {lost his temper} and shouted at the players.
wrong: He lost his temper and stayed perfectly calm.

words.meaning: To say clearly what you believe and defend it publicly.
examples: The students {took a stand} against the new fees.
wrong: She took a stand by keeping her opinion to herself.

words.meaning: To fail to reach a level or goal.
examples: Sales {fell short of} our target this month.
wrong: The results fell short of the goal, beating it by miles.

words.meaning: To try hard to make someone do something.
examples: His parents {put pressure on} him to study medicine.
wrong: They put pressure on her by letting her choose freely.

words.meaning: To not follow the usual rule in one case.
examples: Dogs aren’t allowed, but we’ll {make an exception} for guide dogs.
wrong: They made an exception and applied the rule as usual.
